quote: More importantly, I realized that I had always known this—that the real memory had always been lurking in a corner of my mind
content: The knew-it-all-along effect runs in the flattering direction. People misremember their earlier state as containing the correct answer, which makes them look wiser. The revision here runs the other way: a flattering story ("I refused a negative-sum game on principle") replaced by an unflattering one ("I didn't want to get hurt"). Self-serving memory biases predict that the flattering version survives, so a revision against one's own interest is the kind reconstructive memory is least likely to produce. The discipline also does not depend on what happened at summer camp. What the essay describes is a skill: noticing the sensation of looking away from a thought and turning back toward it. Whether the camp memory is accurate or partly rebuilt, the sensation at fifteen was real, and the skill was learned from it.

quote: Now I’m going to notice every time I do that, and clean out all my corners!
content: The glance is available, and the thought-suppression literature says why. Wegner's ironic-process work found that suppressing a thought requires a monitoring process that keeps searching for it, so the forbidden content keeps flickering at the edge of awareness and rebounds when effort lapses (Wegner et al. 1987). That is the essay's "my mental eye glancing at it for a fraction of a second and then looking away." Anderson and Green's subjects suppressed deliberately, on instruction, which shows the process is one people can do and notice themselves doing (Anderson & Green 2001). The label is fair to query, and "self-serving memory" is the better term. The phenomenon, a flinch that can be caught, is documented.
